title: On the Road's 120-foot scroll
hook: Jack Kerouac typed On the Road on one continuous roll of paper.
peek: In April 1951, Jack Kerouac taped long sheets of paper into a single roll so he would never have to stop to change pages. In about three weeks he typed the first draft of On the Road onto a scroll roughly 120 feet long.
lede: Jack Kerouac had been trying to write his road novel for years. In April 1951, in a New York apartment, he taped together long sheets of thin paper into one continuous roll and fed it through his typewriter. Without pausing to change pages, he typed the whole first draft of On the Road in about three weeks. The scroll is roughly 120 feet long.

bullets.text: The scroll draft is single-spaced and has no paragraph breaks, one long block of text. It also used the real names of Kerouac's friends, such as Neal Cassady, who became Dean Moriarty in the novel.
Publishers were not keen on the draft. The book that finally appeared in 1957 had been heavily revised, with paragraphs, pseudonyms and many passages cut or softened.
The last stretch of the scroll is missing. A note in Kerouac's hand says it was eaten by a friend's dog, and the scroll today ends in a ragged edge.
In 2001 the scroll sold at auction for about 2.4 million dollars to Jim Irsay, owner of the Indianapolis Colts. It has since toured museums, and the scroll version was published as a book in 2007.
